I'm in London as I write this, with plans to stay in Europe another month. I definitely disagree about abandoning Western Europe in the summer; the key, rather, is remaining flexible. While this may be overkill, I have at least three backup destinations set in case of heat domes in parts of Europe.

I was supposed to go to Paris next week, but with high temps once again expected to hit 100º or nearly so, I opted for Porto in northern Portugal instead, where highs should be in the mid-70s – though it was admittedly my third backup. The first one was Berlin, but temps there will be in the 90s again by the end of next week. The second was Innsbruck, but despite its altitude it'll be even hotter than Berlin.

More generally, it's always good to know which European countries – aside from exorbitantly priced Scandinavia & Finland – nearly always have moderate weather, even during the recent summers plagued by heat domes. London's unseasonably warm, but most of the rest of the UK – including all of Scotland and Northern Ireland – is pleasantly cool, as are northern Portugal & northwestern Spain.

Finally, my fourth backup – on the off chance Porto would be hot – was Estonia. It's gorgeous and cool this time of year, as is neighboring Latvia. It's definitely aggravating to keep having to check the weather while on vacation, but nowadays it's ever more essential.

Hug the shady side of the street. Head inside for the main midday meal by 2pm. Follow up with a siesta. The empty virtue signalling aside, what makes me most uncomfortable about land acknowledgement and the guilt of stolen land is the implication that we don't have a legitimate relationship or claim to the lands of the U.S. despite the fact that for the vast majority of ús who aren't immigrants, this is the only land that we have ever known, and for some of ús this has now been the case for 300+ years. At what point does this become our ancestral land too? And how can we have a real connection with land if we're constantly supposed to think of ourselves as colonizers and outsiders? 

None of this is to whitewash the violent actions and erasure of the US government and many settlers against Native nations. That should be taught and talked about, and maybe that's all land acknowledgements are trying to do. But I think the discomfort that even Indigenous people feel with them means they're not hitting the mark.

Back when I was running an educational org in my city we were collecting stories of people who had made a positive impact in the region.  We found it almost impossible to find stories of Native Americans.   It was at this time that I started learning about the specific people who lived in our area- Choctaw and Quapaw- and land acknowledgements started happening.  

I found land acknowledgement a compelling step in the right direction- against the erasure of a people who are not just in our past.  

We also started learning about the Maine- Wabanaki Truth and Reconciliation Commision that addressed the forced removal of Native American children into the foster care system.  We screened the excellent film Dawnland about it. 

To me, the TRC  felt like an even better step in a long process.  I hope there are more of them. 

Thank you for the article and perspective.

comments.name: WE Smith
comments.body: The First Peoples groups displaced from lands by Euro-descendant people in the 17th - 19th centuries had almost certainly, at some point before that, taken those territories by force from some other group of indigenous Americans. Yet you can bet they didn't perform land acknowledgement ceremonies. Instead they celebrated while displaying the scalps of the defeated and raping the women they had captured. Virtue signaling about the past is an incoherent exercise that serves no useful purpose but only gins up a plastic sense of outrage or imposed guilt. Fortunately today most organized societies---Putin's Russia excepted---do not grab one anothers' territories (or mount raids to steal horses or kidnap women). In the past, however, these behaviors were universal, including among Native American groups. We can and should decry such practices, but let's do it in an even-handed fashion, rather than pretend that only Euro-descendant people engaged in them while others were spotless angels.

The notion that land that was once occupied by indigenous people is “stolen” is not one that should be taken seriously today. No, we are not “guests” on of North America; we own the land in a much fuller sense than any Native American ever did, especially since according to this author ownership is a Western social construct. If the Native people never had the concept of owning the land, then how could we have stolen it from them, if we assumed a relationship with the land that they never had in the first place? 

If the US is stolen land, then so is Britain. It was stolen by the Normans in 1066 when they invaded and dispossessed the Anglo Saxons. But actually the Anglo Saxons stole it centuries earlier when they invaded. But still then, it was stolen by the Romans from the Celts. But even the Celts stole it before that. 

The notion of “stolen land” and that we, Americans, are “guests” in our own country ignores the fact that men have moved around, conquered, settled, and dispossessed each other for all time. That doesn’t mean it’s good or okay, but it does mean that it is ludicrous to suggest that there is anything illegitimate about our ownership of this land today.

Supplements won’t undo, bad habits, like excessive drinking or high sugar intake. But I take issue with the idea that they are wholly unhelpful for detoxifying the body.

I’m a nurse practitioner, so I do have professional basis for pushing back here.

What is frequently disregarded when people say things like, “the liver detoxifies itself, it doesn’t need a cleanse” is that the body is dealing with things that it has never before in human history had to metabolize and excrete. We are exposed daily to a laundry list of chemicals and toxins, some of which are very difficult for the body to eliminate.

Things like milk thistle have a long history of efficacy in improving liver health. There’s generally no harm in supporting the body with some high-quality supplements that can support the body in doing its job in today’s modern world. I wish the media would stop finding medical professionals who hold a hardline stance that supplements are unproven and unhelpful. They’re doing a discredit to people who could genuinely benefit from some of these supplements.

If one can’t afford supplements, then it’s obviously OK to skip them. But if you have the means to incorporate some relevant supplements, the risk versus reward is often favorable. Of course every individual is different, and what makes sense for one person might not make sense for another. Focusing on high-quality supplements with some clinical research behind it is key. Look for cGMP certification and third-party testing.

Some of it is so bad, no wonder artists aren't concerned. Some others though, compete directly with the remixes made by the artists or their studios themselves. I'm a copyright law professor. Composers make money by licensing the copyright to their compositions. Music (or art or text) generated by AI is not copyrightable without significant human authored expression ( and no, the Copright Office has pointed out, a prompt is not the same thing as human expression).

And if it's not copyrightable, it can't be licensed because it's free for anybody to use. Which eliminates licensing as a source of revenue, leaving only ad revenue from online engagement, which is far less money.

All of that means even if we put aside the aesthetic, an artistic issues of Gen-AI, it's a bad deal for anyone depending upon royalties and licensing... such as the entire music, TV, and film industries.

But none of that information is contained in this article that seems designed to kiss up to tech bros by failing to address the real issues the creative industries are concerned about.

Nuclear power plants are just ridiculously expensive.  

A natural gas power plant costs less than one-tenth and takes a small fraction of time to build compared to nuclear. And the nuclear requires much more expensive ongoing investment related to equipment, re-fueling, and spent fuel management during its life cycle.  So until there are disruptive breakthroughs on costs (tried many times without success), nuclear is to remain a minor baseload power source.  

There’s a reason why China has 1100 coal fired power plants in operation and continues to build hundreds more each year, vs. 62 nuclear plants in operation and a few dozen in construction.  (Unfortunately for China and world climate, they do not have significant natural gas reserves, so they are left primarily with coal by default for baseload power.  By the way, the US generates more power from solar than from coal.  Solar surpassed coal in May 2026.  China generates over 55% of their power from coal vs. 11% from solar.)

Renewables are great, but capacity increases are incremental and baseload power is needed to fill in gaps in the highly variable output.  That’s where natural gas comes in in the US and coal in China.

Killer Whales. That's what they are and well deserved. No greater top marine predator.

Orca? Latin. Translated into Death Whale. Feel better about attempting to cutify a such a deadly mammal? The genus name Orcinus means "of the kingdom of the dead", or "belonging to Orcus". Ancient Romans originally used orca (pl. orcae) for these animals, possibly borrowing Ancient Greek ὄρυξ (óryx), which referred (among other things) to a whale species.

A further misnomer is that these are dolphins and therefore not whales. Incorrect, as all species within infraorder Cetacean are whales. Cetaceans are divided into two parvorders - Mysticeti (baleen whales) and Odontoceti (toothed whales). Within that latter order of whales, 6 species within Dolphinoidea (dolphins) have 'whale,' including killer whales, within their common names.

Both the Russian doctrine of deep operations (multi front, echelons) and the Ukrainian maneuver counteroffensive have been neutralized. The resulting drone-patrolled no man’s land at the line of contact has led to various tactical innovations but no enduring decisive campaign on either side.

This interregnum of pure attritional warfare, redolent of last century’s trenches has elevated the value of technological innovation and its operational and strategic use. This is where the true evolution is starting, and also why flexible general officers, like Drapatiy are needed.

With the near battlespace suffused with drones, the deep strikes into Russian territory and specifically their varied launch points holds the key to effecting an economic and strategic gut punch on the bear. Cutting off supply and energy flows to Crimea, oil refineries deep in the vast Russian hinterlands, and consequently reminding the population of its participation in this special military operation are in effect the hallmarks of any strategic bombing campaign since WWII.

The trajectory of both sides, given these new strategic gambits, will lean towards long range drones, ballistic missiles, and their associated air defense counter assets. But as we know, no war has been won with air power alone. And it remains to be seen if a durable peace can be achieved from an exhausted stalemate.

What strikes me about this article is how each culture and each generation has adapted a universally relevant human story to speak to their own time. 

Homer based his epics on stories of a bygone age.  While some of the details of life in the Mycenean period, which is when, Odysseus, if he was based on a real man, would have lived, are surprisingly accurate, he probably changed things around a little to make the story relevant to his much audience the way that medieval poets dressed King Arthur, another man who may or may not have lived, in plate armor.

Greeks saw Odysseus as one of their own: supersmart, brave and capable.  The Romans too saw him as a typical Greek too, smart yes, but a little too slippery to be trusted.

In "Ulysses", the 1950s movie starring Kirk Douglas, he's a fairly uncomplicated hero battling gods and monsters to get home from a war0--a story which resonated with the generation which had won World War II.

Fast forward to the mid 2020s and decades of "forever wars".   

In "The Odyssey" and "The Return" starring Ralph Fiennes, Odysseus is portrayed as a warrior wracked with guilt for what he did in a long war launched by arrogant and foolish leaders. 

There are elements of this in Homer, but previous generations chose to downplay this aspect of the story.   It speaks to our own times however, or at least to some of us.  The online right hates this take on the hero but absolutely loves the earlier "Ulysses".  

That too speaks to our times too.

The coasts are only one part of the danger. Flash flooding inundates the antiquated sewer system so much that even when sewer drains are clear of debris the water has nowhere to go but into the streets and people’s basements. There are many proven methods of dealing with this, such as porous sidewalks, or using recessed playgrounds and parks to divert and store the water. But instead the city just keeps rolling along with the old ways of doing things, as if flooding never happens. In my neighborhood they recently tore up porous paver sidewalks and replaced them with non permeable concrete, and redid a basketball court but didn’t recess it. It’s like the city bureaucracy is moving backwards instead of forwards “because that’s the way we’ve always done it.”

I’m sorry to say it but this is the kind of problem that requires an experienced leader who can steer all the city agencies toward shared goals. Mamdani is a nice guy but he doesn’t understand how to lead a large organization. 

We can’t wait another eight years.

What this article misstates what is meant by "affordable housing".

The true measure is whether there is adequate housing available in a given region that costs no more than about 1/3 the median income.

I live in Manhattan and, yes, I meet the criteria in this article.

But Manhattan is not a separate region or jurisdiction.  It is a part of NYC that is, itself, a part of a larger metropolitan region.

Moreover, this article simply measure housing cost on the basis of home ownership.

But NYC, including Manhattan, remains a city with a large number of residents living in rental housing.

On that basis, the amount of income needed to rent an apartment in Manhattan is now far greater than this "ownership-based" analysis shows.

For Manhattan, and the greater NY region to thrive it needs to provide rental housing that is, indeed, "affordable".

The most important mechanism used to attempt to achieve that is to provide incentives for developers to build residences with mixed-income components.

In return for various zoning and tax incentives developers set aside a certain proportion of total units that are affordable to primarily middle-income NY'ers.

These units are rentals that may be a portion of a total rental project where the bulk of the apartments are "market".  Or they may be a rental component of a building where the other units are market-rate condos.

The challenge is to build affordable rental housing.

This analysis fails to understand that.
